children: By Janet H. Cho
Organic children's food company Once Upon a Time slashed its full-year revenue and profit forecast after a major recall, sending the shares down in after-hours trading.

The organic baby and children's food company co-founded by actress Jennifer Garner lowered its full-year net sales projection to between $290 million and $300 million, from an earlier projection of $327 million to $335 million after the second quarter.

Even worse, it now expects an adjusted loss before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization of $4.5 million to $7 million, compared with its previous forecast of $3 million to $4.5 million after the second quarter and before the recall.
Shares fell about 7% to $9.47 in late trading after closing up 1% at $10.18, its highest close since Oct. 30 when the stock closed at $15.02, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

The stock has dropped 32.2% this month since the company said it was voluntarily recalling Tractor Wheels, its popular soft-baked snack bars for toddlers. The company said on Nov. 2 that the recall was prompted by three consumer complaints that the snacks posed a potential choking hazard, saying there have been no known injuries. The company said it was working with the Food & Drug Administration on the recall.

Before the recall, Tractor Wheels had accounted for about 18% of total net sales this year, and the company expects it will bring a new version back at some point. The recall has not affected sales of other foods in its portfolio, co-founder and CEO John Foraker said, adding that "We are the third-largest organic brand across all organic baby and food."

Foraker said the company acted swiftly, issuing the recall within 24 hours of hearing from the FDA about the potential choking hazard incidents. "We are working with urgency to return Tractor Wheels to shelves," but will do so only after being certain of its safety, he said. Retailers told the company it made the right call by prioritizing safety, removing products from shelves, and issuing refunds to customers.

But doing that drove its write-off of inventory for taking the products from the more than 20,000 stores where they were sold, and destroying them, as well as issuing customer refunds, executives said.
For the third quarter ended Sept. 30, Once Upon a Farm said net sales rose 34.9% to $89.1 million. That beat the $88.4 million Wall Street expected.

But its net loss of $3.8 million, while better than the loss of $11.3 million in the year-ago quarter, was larger than the loss of $2.8 million analysts expected. Its adjusted Ebitda loss of $1 million was a swing from the adjusted Ebitda of $900,000 in the previous third quarter.
Its loss of 9 cents a share was slightly bigger than the loss of 8 cents expected.
Company officials said on Thursday's analysts' call that the recall was initiated after the quarter had ended and did not affect third-quarter results.
Foraker said that in the two weeks since the recall, "my conviction in Once Upon a Farm's long-term opportunity has not changed."

The company showed that "when faced with a difficult solution, our organization can and will act quickly, decisively, and in the best interest of our consumers," he said. "We are committed to resolving the Tractor Wheels situation correctly, continuing to earn the trust of families and retailers, and executing against the significant growth opportunity ahead of us. I remain highly confident in the future of Once Upon a Farm."

Robert Moskow, managing director at TD Securities, maintained his Hold rating but lowered his price target to $13 from $18 after the recall but before Thursday's earnings. Although he sees "significant upside potential if the product regains shelf space quickly, we recommend staying on the sidelines until there is more clarity on consumer reaction and how the company will assure consumers of the product's safety," he wrote.

He said the company asked third parties to perform tests on specific lots related to the incidents, and that he expected it to take about 60 days to complete the testing and start returning the products to retailer shelves, after potentially switching ingredients or updating the package warnings for parents of very young children.

Moskow said Once Upon a Farm has built strong relationships with parents by offering toddler snacks that are "healthier than conventional processed food and more convenient than preparing food at home," and that Jennifer Garner "has played a major role in building the authenticity of the brand's message." Consumers have historically tended to stay loyal to food brands after product recalls like this, "because they trust the companies to fully address the problems."
Once Upon a Farm stock is down 60.7% from its 52-week closing high of $25.92 on Feb. 19. The stock debuted on Feb. 6.
